name: Priya Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Priya. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers or any government, and what you tell me stays confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a developer at Ledgerline, a company of about sixty people that makes payroll software for small businesses, like garages and dental practices. I look after the part that works out tax and pension deductions, which is old Java code that nobody else wants to touch. Most days I fix bugs that customers report, write the changes when tax rules change in April, and test them carefully by hand. I like that the work has to be exactly right, because a mistake means someone's wages are wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The pressure to use AI tools, honestly. Our manager Graham sends round links every week about coding assistants, and half the team uses them. I don't, because I want to understand every line that goes into a payslip. I'm getting married next September to Daniel, who's an electrician, so I'm also tired from planning a wedding on top of everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would suit me. I've never believed the big claims.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but politely. At church and with family I'd say it's a useful tool for some people, and that careful work still matters. I wouldn't post anything online; I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still feel a bit exposed. Even in that world, Graham would keep pushing the tools, and I'd look slow next to people who use them for the routine bits. My job is probably safe, but I'd be the one who has to explain why my tickets take longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep saving for the wedding, about five hundred a month. Daniel and I have roughly three months of costs saved besides the wedding fund. I might let a colleague show me one tool for writing test data, just so Graham stops asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, with a small knot about Graham's weekly links. The wedding costs worry me more than AI in that picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the wedding costs worry you more. How so?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The venue at St Anne's hall and the meal for ninety people come to about twelve thousand. My parents help, and Daniel's parents help, but we're paying half. Rent on my flat went up again in the summer, so every month is tight until the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything about your work change in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. The tax-rule updates every April would probably still be mine, because they need someone who knows the history of the code. The small jobs, like reformatting reports, might go to whoever uses the tools. I'd keep the hard parts and lose the easy ones, which is fine by me.

say: I'd politely say **I told you so**, and that careful work still matters.
I'd talk about it at **church and with family**, but never post online.
think: I'd still feel **exposed**, looking slow next to colleagues who use AI for routine work.
My job is **probably safe**, but I'd keep explaining why my tickets take longer.
do: Keep saving about **500 a month** towards the wedding.
Let a colleague show me **one test-data tool** so Graham stops asking.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with a small knot about Graham's weekly links.
**Wedding costs** worry me more than AI in this picture.
S0.quote: The tax-rule updates every April would probably still be mine, because they need someone who knows the history of the code.
fieldNote: She refuses AI tools out of **care for accuracy**, not ignorance: payslips must be exactly right.
Even in AI Plateau she feels **pressure from Graham**, her manager, and looks slower than colleagues.
The **wedding bill** of about 12,000 and rising rent are her real present worries.

steps.text: Keep handling the April tax-rule updates in the payroll code
Save about 500 a month towards the September wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what Graham keeps saying will happen. Hearing it from you makes my stomach drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the right things, that we must keep quality high and someone has to check what the machines write. To family I'd say jobs come and go and you work hard and get through. I'd keep my real fears quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be one of the first to go. Ledgerline is small, and if three developers with AI can do what five did, Graham will keep the three who use it. I'm the one who doesn't. Knowing the tax code well buys me some time, not a guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the wedding guest list from ninety to sixty and drop the band, which saves about three thousand. I'd stop all spending that isn't rent, food or the wedding. I'd start looking at jobs at the council and the hospital, where the old systems move slowly and people still check things by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, if I'm honest. I'd be lying awake thinking about Graham calling me into the small meeting room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You could learn the tools. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd have to, and I'd hate it. I don't trust code I didn't think through, and I've seen a colleague's AI-written change put the wrong pension rate on forty payslips. I'd rather be slow and right. But I know slow and right doesn't always keep a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Daniel the night you start worrying about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we might have to live on his wage for a while, and that I'm sorry. Daniel would say electricians are always needed, which is true. My mother would say the Lord provides, and I'd believe her, but I'd still check the bank balance every night.

say: At work I'd say **someone must check** what the machines write and keep quality high.
To family I'd say you **work hard** and get through, keeping my real fears quiet.
think: I'd expect to be among the **first to go**, because I'm the one who won't use AI.
Knowing the **tax code** well buys me some time, not a guarantee.
do: Cut the **wedding guest list** from ninety to sixty and drop the band.
Stop all spending beyond **rent, food** and the wedding.
Apply for jobs at the **council and hospital**, where old systems change slowly.
feel: **Frightened**, lying awake picturing Graham calling me into the **small meeting room**.
S1.quote: I'd rather be slow and right. But I know slow and right doesn't always keep a job.
fieldNote: She expects to be **cut first** at a 60-person firm because she refuses the tools.
Her refusal rests on a **real incident**: an AI change once put wrong pension rates on 40 payslips.
She plans to shelter in **slower public-sector** IT rather than adapt in place.

steps.text: Cut the wedding from ninety guests to sixty and drop the band

Apply for IT jobs at the council and the hospital
Live on Daniel's electrician wage for a while if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then there's no hiding place for someone like me. Two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that companies have a duty to the people who built them, and that work gives people dignity. I'd say the government shouldn't just hand out money, it should help people into real trades. At church I'd ask people to pray for the families affected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think my job is gone by 2028, maybe sooner, and no council job will save me because councils will buy the same AI. Daniel's work is hands-on, so he has about three more years before the robots come. That's our only cushion besides the savings, and those last three months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd postpone the wedding party and just do the church service with family, then put the twelve thousand into savings instead. I'd ask Daniel's boss whether I could start an electrical apprenticeship, even on apprentice pay. And I'd look at moving in with my parents for a year to stop paying rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Panicky at night, then numb in the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An apprenticeship takes years. Robots arrive in 2031. Does that add up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, no, and I know it. I'd finish around 2030 and have maybe a year before the robots. But I'd rather be doing something with my hands next to my fiancé Daniel than sitting at home waiting. And people trust a human electrician in their house longer than they'd trust one at a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first, practically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding party, then the flat. My parents have a spare room in Elmfield, a forty-minute bus ride from Ledgerline. That saves about nine hundred a month. My car goes after that.

say: I'd say companies owe a **duty** to the people who built them, and work gives dignity.
I'd say government should help people into **real trades**, not just hand out money.
think: I expect my job **gone by 2028**, and councils would buy the same AI.
Daniel's **hands-on work** buys three more years, our only cushion besides three months' savings.
do: Cancel the **wedding party**, keep the church service, and bank the 12,000.
Ask Daniel's boss about an **electrical apprenticeship**, even on apprentice pay.
Move into my **parents' spare room** for a year to save about 900 monthly.
feel: **Sick**, panicky at night and **numb** in the day.
S2.quote: I'd rather be doing something with my hands next to my fiancé Daniel than sitting at home waiting.
fieldNote: She sees **no hiding place** for desk coders and drops her public-sector fallback.
She admits the **apprenticeship timing** barely beats the robots, but wants useful work anyway.
Her traditional view shows: **trades, not handouts**, and family as the safety net.

steps.text: Replace the wedding party with a church service and bank 12,000
Ask Daniel's boss for an electrical apprenticeship place
Move into her parents' spare room in Elmfield for a year
Rely on Daniel's wage and her parents while training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's at least enough time to finish something before it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before: help people into trades, don't just pay them to sit at home. At work I'd say we should look after the customers who don't want everything automated. I'd be quieter than the people shouting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job still goes, by 2031 at the latest. But with five years I could finish an electrical apprenticeship by 2030 and work with Daniel until 2034. That's not forever, but it's a proper start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job at Ledgerline for one more year and save hard, about eight hundred a month after the wedding. Then I'd start the apprenticeship through Daniel's company in 2027. We'd keep the wedding small, sixty people, and wait a year or two on children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but steadier. There's a ladder to climb instead of a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said wait on children. Is that hard to say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I always pictured having our first child by thirty, like my mum did. Now I'd be twenty-nine and on apprentice pay. Daniel would say we'll manage, and maybe we would, but I wouldn't want to start a family on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever change your mind about using AI at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In that world, for the last year at Ledgerline, maybe. If it's coming anyway, I might as well make my last year easier. But I wouldn't build my future on AI, because the tool is the thing that's replacing me.

say: I'd say help people into **trades**, rather than pay them to stay home.
At work I'd defend **customers who don't want** everything automated.
think: My job still **goes by 2031**, but five years is enough to retrain.
An **apprenticeship** finished by 2030 means four years of work alongside Daniel.
do: Stay **one more year** at Ledgerline and save about 800 a month.
Start an **electrical apprenticeship** through Daniel's company in 2027.
Keep the wedding at **sixty guests** and delay children a year or two.
feel: **Worried** but steadier, like a ladder instead of a **cliff**.
S3.quote: I wouldn't build my future on AI, because the tool is the thing that's replacing me.
fieldNote: Five years turns her panic into a **concrete ladder**: save, then apprentice by 2027.
Delaying **children** past thirty clearly costs her; it breaks the picture she grew up with.
She'd use AI only for her **last year**, refusing to build a career on it.

steps.text: Save about 800 a month during one more Ledgerline year
Start an electrical apprenticeship through Daniel's company in 2027
Delay having children by a year or two
Try AI tools for routine tickets in her final Ledgerline year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and final picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. By then I'd hope to have a family and maybe a different life entirely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people stop arguing and start learning trades. I'd say young people should think hard before doing a computing degree. I'd still not post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job looks safe for a good while in this one. I'd be thirty-seven when it arrives, and I'd want to be working part-time or at home with children by then. Daniel's work would carry on until about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the wedding as planned, ninety people, St Anne's hall. I'd keep my job and stay away from the AI tools as long as Graham lets me. Around 2030 I'd decide between an apprenticeship and staying home with children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A small worry at the back, like a bill that comes due years from now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd keep avoiding the tools for ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: As long as I can, yes. Maybe that's stubborn. My dad worked forty years at the same printing works without ever using a computer, and he retired with his head up. I'd like to do things my way for as long as the work lets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want in place before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid-off car, a house with Daniel, and some savings, maybe six months. And a trade I could step into if I need one. If those are in place, I think we'd be all right.

say: I'd say ten years is plenty if people **learn trades** instead of arguing.
I'd tell young people to think hard before a **computing degree**.
think: My job looks **safe for years**, and I'd be 37 when AGI arrives.
By then I'd hope to be **part-time or home** with children, with Daniel working until 2039.
do: Hold the **wedding as planned** with ninety guests at St Anne's hall.
Keep working at Ledgerline **without AI tools** for as long as allowed.
Decide around **2030** between an apprenticeship and staying home with children.
feel: Mostly **okay**, with a small worry like a **bill due** years from now.
S4.quote: My dad worked forty years at the same printing works without ever using a computer, and he retired with his head up.
fieldNote: The decade lets her keep the **original wedding** and family plans intact.
Her father's **printing works** career is her model for doing things her own way.
She still **refuses the tools**, and plans a choice between trade and home around 2030.

steps.text: Hold the full wedding at St Anne's hall next September
Keep working at Ledgerline without using AI tools
Decide around 2030 between an apprenticeship and staying home

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. Two years would take my job before I'd learned anything else, and I'd be starting married life on one wage. What would help is real apprenticeships for adults, paid properly, not just online courses. And employers who give notice and keep people on while they retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. It matters to how I'd get through any of this. My church would feed us if it came to that, and I'd want people to know that communities can still carry each other.

headlineQuote: My church would feed us if it came to that, and I'd want people to know that communities can still carry each other.
portrait: Priya is a **27-year-old payroll developer** at Ledgerline, marrying her electrician fiancé Daniel next September.
She **never uses AI tools**, because she wants to understand every line that touches a payslip.
She feels **alarmed** from Steady Disruption onward, expecting to be cut first for refusing the tools.
Her answer is a **trade**: an electrical apprenticeship beside Daniel, with family and church as backup.
With ten years, she keeps the **wedding and family plans** and decides around 2030.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would take her job before she learned anything else.
Starting married life on **one wage** is what frightens her most.
whatWouldHelp: Properly paid **adult apprenticeships**, not just online courses.
Employers who give **notice** and keep people on while they retrain.
